newsitem.title: GHANA: Ghana opposition pledges privatised cocoa exports.
newsitem.headline: Ghana opposition pledges privatised cocoa exports.

text.p: Ghana's leading opposition New Patriotic Party (NPP) will privatise cocoa exports and increase farmgate prices if it wins next month's presidential and general elections, according to its manifesto.

"The NPP will move forward to privatise the external marketing of cocoa under conditions which will ensure maintenance of quality control and development of cocoa processing and related activities," the manifesto says.
At present, the state-run Cocoa Marketing Board (COCOBOD) has the monopoly on cocoa exports.

Foreign diplomats and other observers predict President Jerry Rawlings will win the December 7 presidential election, but by a narrow margin, and they do not totally exclude a win by the NPP's John Kufuor.
Kufuor's chances of winning grew after his party formed an alliance with the People's Convention Party (PCP). The result of the parliamentary poll is even more uncertain.
The Rawlings government has been dragging its feet over privatisation of cocoa exports.
Finance Minister Kwame Peprah recently told Reuters that his ministry was studying proposals in that direction made by a British consultant hired by the World Bank.

In its manifesto the ruling National Democratic Congress does not mention privatisation of exports. It does, however, pledge to increase cocoa farmgate prices to between 55 and 65 percent of the Free on Board (FOB) export price by the year 2000.
At a recent rally, the NPP's presidential candidate promised to raise farmgate prices to 75 percent of the FOB price.

Currently Ghana's cocoa farmers receive 52 percent of the FOB price but a World Bank report in April said inflation and depreciation of the cedi currency had cut the value to farmers to about 40 percent of the Janauary 1996 FOB price.
Experts blame low farmgate prices for Ghanaian yields of just 200 kg/hectare, only two thirds of those in neighbouring Ivory Coast, the world's top producer.
The report also blames low prices for the fact that trees in Ghana are allowed to grow too old and for untimely application of fungicides and pesticides.
In Cameroon, farmers receive some 73 percent of the FOB price and in Nigeria 80 percent. Cameroon liberalised cocoa marketing in 1993, Nigeria in 1986.
Farmgate prices in Indonesia and Malaysia are about 80 percent and 90 percent respectively, according to the report.
